summary: Defines the second version of the Management Information Base for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets, working with the structure rules in RFC 1155 and the protocol in RFC 1157. It is on the standards track. It was replaced by RFC 1213.

plainLanguage.summary: The checklist of facts a device can report, in a newer and longer edition than the first one.

subtitle: The vocabulary of facts a managed TCP/IP device must report

tldr.problem: Network administrators need a standard way to check the health and activity of routers, servers, and other devices. Each vendor uses different methods and data formats, making monitoring difficult.
tldr.mechanism: MIB-II defines a set of standard managed objects (variables) that every TCP/IP device can report, including system info, interface statistics, and protocol counters. SNMP uses this vocabulary to query devices.
tldr.outcome: MIB-II became the foundation for network management in TCP/IP networks throughout the 1990s. It was replaced by RFC 1213, which clarified ASN.1 syntax.

today: RFC 1158 is a Proposed Standard that was replaced by RFC 1213, which clarified ASN.1 syntax and improved the specification format. MIB-II remains foundational to SNMP-based network management.

sections.title: Overview of MIB-II
sections.content:
MIB stands for Management Information Base. MIB-II is the second version of the standard set of information that TCP/IP devices (routers, servers, hosts) must report when asked.

MIB-II is the vocabulary part of network management. When paired with the SNMP protocol (which asks the questions) and the SMI structure definition (which says how to organize the data), it provides a complete system for monitoring and controlling networks. Every IP and TCP implementation should be manageable via MIB-II and SNMP.

This RFC extends MIB-I (its predecessor) with new objects to meet operational needs that arose as the Internet grew. It remains upwards compatible: all MIB-I objects are still present.
sections.plainLanguage: MIB-II is the manual that says what information a network device must be able to report, like "how many packets came in" or "is this port up or down."

sections.title: Ten Groups of Managed Objects
sections.content:
MIB-II organizes objects into ten groups, each covering a different aspect of a managed device.

System: basic facts about the device such as uptime, contact person, location, and what services it offers (physical layer, datalink, IP, TCP, applications).

Interfaces: for each network port (Ethernet, serial line, etc.), statistics like speed, MTU size, and counts of packets sent and received, including errors.

Address Translation: the old table mapping IP addresses to MAC addresses (deprecated in MIB-II but kept for compatibility). New objects in the IP group replace it.

IP: datagram forwarding statistics, routing table, fragment reassembly, and the updated address translation table specific to IP.

ICMP, TCP, UDP, EGP: protocol-specific counters and state tables for each protocol layer.

Transmission: reserved namespace for media-specific objects added by future RFCs.

SNMP: statistics about SNMP itself (how many requests received, authentication failures, etc.).
sections.plainLanguage: The ten groups are like sections of a dashboard: system info, interfaces (ports), IP stats, TCP stats, UDP stats, etc. Each section has numbers to track.

sections.title: System and Interfaces Group Examples
sections.content:
The System group is mandatory for all devices. It includes sysDescr (a text description of the device), sysUpTime (how long it has been running since last reboot), and sysServices (a bitmask of layers the device operates at).

The Interfaces group is also mandatory. For each interface, it tracks ifSpeed (the link speed), ifMtu (maximum packet size), and ifAdminStatus and ifOperStatus (desired and actual state, such as up, down, or testing). It also maintains counters of octets and packets sent and received, both successfully and with errors.

The interface table is keyed by ifIndex, a simple integer. An Ethernet port might have ifIndex 2, a serial line ifIndex 3, and so on. This allows management stations to refer to interfaces by number even when the device is rebooted.
sections.plainLanguage: System tells you about the whole machine (what it is, how long it has been running). Interfaces tells you about each port: is it up, how many packets arrived, how many had errors.

sections.title: IP and Higher-Layer Protocol Objects
sections.content:
The IP group tracks the flow of IP datagrams. ipInReceives counts all datagrams received, ipInDelivers counts successful deliveries to upper layers, and ipInDiscards counts packets dropped (e.g., for lack of buffer space). Separate counters track header errors, bad addresses, and unknown protocols.

ipForwarding is read-write: setting it to 1 turns the device into a router; setting it to 2 makes it a plain host. The device maintains a routing table and can report via ipRoutingTable which routes are configured, with subnet mask support added in MIB-II.

The TCP group maintains a connection table: for each active TCP session, the table lists the local and remote address and port, plus connection state (closed, listen, established, etc.). Counters track segments received and sent, retransmissions, and errors.

The UDP group lists active UDP listeners (ports receiving datagrams), allowing administrators to see what services are active on the device.
sections.plainLanguage: IP counters tell you how many packets arrived, how many were delivered, how many had errors. TCP shows active connections. UDP shows listening ports.

sections.title: Implementation Requirements and Compatibility
sections.content:
System and Interfaces groups are mandatory: every IP device must implement them. The IP group is mandatory. The TCP, UDP, and ICMP groups must be implemented if those protocols are in use.

An object may be read-only or read-write. A read-write object like ifAdminStatus allows a management station to change the device's behavior, such as disabling a port. Read-only objects like counters allow monitoring but not control.

MIB-II uses a format called ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One) to define objects precisely. Each object has a syntax (integer, counter, string, etc.), semantics (what it measures), and a unique numeric identifier in an object identifier tree. This machine-readable format allows software tools to automatically generate management code.

The RFC is designed for multi-vendor networks where devices from different manufacturers must be manageable by the same tools. Upwards compatibility with MIB-I ensures that management stations built for the older standard can still work with newer devices.
sections.plainLanguage: Every device must support System and Interfaces. If a device uses IP, it must support the IP group. Read-only objects show information; read-write objects let you change settings.
